title: Nissan-Based Pickup Among New Mitsubishi Models to Arrive by 2030

body_markdown:
It’s not too far-fetched to argue that Mitsubishi[lost its way](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/mitsubishi-had-the-perfect-lineup-in-1992/) in the United States. The brand consigned its performance DNA to the automotive attic when it axed the Lancer Evolution in 2015, and in spite of[its vast off-roading heritage](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/1985-dakar-winning-mitsubishi-pajero-restored/) , it has so far missed the opportunity to capitalize on the booming demand for adventurous SUVs. Brighter days are ahead: Several new Mitsubishi models are coming here by 2030.


The company published an updated version of an ambitious business plan called Momentum 2030 that’s based around four pillars: Electrification, an expanded product range, a modernized retail sales model, and sustainable sales growth. While numerous details remain under wraps, Mitsubishi clarified that it’s betting on several new models to re-establish its place in the mainstream American market. Mitsubishi will also rely on corporate partner Nissan and its economies of scale to fast-track new vehicles to dealer lots.


An image published by the brand partially reveals what its product portfolio will look like in the coming years. Pictured below, it shows six models that are shrouded in darkness. Given the partnership with Nissan, some are relatively easy to recognize. The one on the bottom left is likely the Eclipse Sportback EV, which is pretty clearly based on[the Nissan Leaf](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-2026-nissan-leaf-electric-small-crossover/) . To the right of it is the Outlander, which is offered as a plug-in hybrid, followed by what could be a new Outlander Sport. Finally, on the far right, there’s what looks like a crossover based on the Nissan Kicks.


Edited with exposure set to max, for your viewing pleasure.


Mitsubishi


Moving to the top, the truck on the left side is a new pickup that will be based on[the Nissan Frontier](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-2025-nissan-frontier-pro-4x-review/) and return Mitsubishi to the pickup segment after a long hiatus. We’re a little puzzled by the SUV next to it, but Mitsubishi identified one of its new models as “a new, rugged Outlander variant.” This could be it. It could land as an option package that adds outdoorsy styling, a lift kit, and meaty tires, or it could arrive as an Outlander-branded offshoot. Regardless, the model is due out by the end of 2027.


There’s not a single sedan, coupe, or wagon pictured in the preview image, and that’s not a coincidence. Mitsubishi stressed that it will focus on “adventure-oriented and off-road-capable vehicles” to win back market share in the United States. Put another way, don’t expect[the tiny Mirage](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/report-mitsubishi-to-kill-mirage-in-u-s/) , which was once both celebrated and vilified as the industry’s value champion, to make a comeback.


It’s still too early to tell whether[the next-generation Montero](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/next-mitsubishi-montero-debut-date/) will be sold in the United States. The big, body-on-frame SUV will make its global debut on September 2, 2026, and it will be sold in numerous global markets (where it’s sometimes called Pajero or Shogun), but the official word from Mitsubishi’s American division is that it hasn’t decided if it will bring the model to our shores.


While there’s no shortage of[rumors](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/next-gen-mitsubishi-lancer-evo-is-a-dream/) detailing a new Lancer Evolution, the model doesn’t appear in Mitsubishi’s product plan, and nothing suggests that it’s in the pipeline. The brand built the last Lancer in 2024, and it hasn’t announced a replacement yet, largely because it plans to focus on more lucrative trucks and SUVs. Without a Lancer, the odds of seeing another Lancer Evo are low.


It sounds like Mitsubishi is serious about earning a bigger share of the U.S. market. Nissan’s role in the Momentum 2030 plan shouldn’t be minimized, however: The brand is working on its own turnaround[after a tumultuous few years](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/new-nissan-ceo-a-car-guy-who-is-full-of-energy-will-that-be-enough/) , and investing in Mitsubishi, which it holds a 24% stake in, is a way to benefit from economies of scale while filling some of the extra capacity in its factories.
